steps.text: The kubelet monitors resources like memory, disk space, and filesystem inodes on your cluster's nodes.
When the monitored resource levels reach specific thresholds, the kubelet can proactively fail one or more pods to reclaim resources and prevent starvation.
The kubelet sets the phase for selected pods to `Failed` and terminates them during a node-pressure eviction.
You can tune the thresholds by configuring your own values or using hard or soft eviction thresholds as per your requirements.

For static pods, you can set the `priority` field to avoid being evicted under resource pressure. However, if a system daemon consumes more resources than reserved via `system-reserved` or `kube-reserved` allocations and there are no other pods using less resources, the kubelet may need to choose to evict one of these pods.

For local ephemeral storage, if the sum of local ephemeral storage usage from all containers and also the Pod's `emptyDir` volumes exceeds the overall Pod storage limit, then the kubelet marks the Pod for eviction. Ensure that the filesystem backing the `emptyDir` volumes provides project quota support.
For API-initiated evictions, you can learn how to protect your applications with a Pod Disruption Budget and about Node-pressure Eviction and Pod Priority and Preemption.
Review the supported configurations for ephemeral local storage and ensure that the kubelet is measuring local ephemeral storage. If not, Pods exceeding their local storage limit will not be evicted.

Set `archive_timeout` to a reasonable value, such as a minute or so, in the `postgresql.conf` file or on the server command line. This parameter can only be set in the `postgresql.conf` file or on the server command line.

Configure WAL archiving by setting up an archive_command that specifies how to copy WAL segments off the primary server, such as using a script or library function. Ensure your archive command can handle filenames up to 64 characters long and includes `%p` for the relative path and `%f` for the file name.

Set `archive_time` in the `postgresql.conf` file or on the server command line, which limits how old unarchived data can be. This parameter is only set at server start and must be reset for any subsequent recovery you wish to perform.

Create a file called `standby.signal` in the data directory if you want to use standby mode, which will allow the server to continue recovery even when the end of archived WAL is reached. Use `restore_command` for fetching new WAL segments as needed during recovery.

Monitor the archiving process to ensure it is working as intended and adjust your archive command or library if necessary to handle file names up to 64 characters long and include `%p` and `%f`. Ensure you have a backup strategy in place for configuration files, since WAL archiving does not restore changes made to these.

For point-in-time recovery, stop the replay at any point to achieve a consistent snapshot of the database as it was at that time. This can be done by stopping the `pg_wal` directory from growing and ensuring you have enough space for archived WAL segments.

Consider using streaming replication instead of archiving if data needs to be copied off the primary server more quickly than what is possible with archiving. This can reduce I/O wait times during recovery, but it may not provide as quick a copy of data as you need.

For continuous backup and point-in-time recovery, ensure your file system snapshot capability or archiving tool supports indefinitely long sequences of WAL files for replay. This allows for the combination of an indefinite sequence of WAL files with a file-system-level backup to achieve continuous backup.

After removing the resource, run `terraform init` to initialize the Terraform configuration again.
Finally, try provisioning your cluster again with `terraform apply`.
